\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
The equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main}
2x^{4}+xy+4y^{3}-1=0
\end{equation}
has no integer solutions.
\end{theorem}

Replacing $y$ by $-y$ transforms \eqref{eq:main} into $f(x,y)=0$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:f}
f(x,y)=4y^3+xy-2x^4+1 .
\end{equation}
We prove that $f(x,y)=0$ has no integer solutions; all statements below refer to the coordinates of \eqref{eq:f}. We also use the coordinate $Y=2y$ and the polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{eq:g}
g(x,Y)=Y^3+xY-4x^4+2=2f(x,Y/2).
\end{equation}

The proof uses one graph of Hilbert symbols of order $8$ over $\Q(\zeta_8)$. Its vertices are 824 lines and their Galois conjugates ($3296$ lines in all), and its 42512 edges sit at 26615 points, the \emph{anchors}, at which two or more lines meet. The graph defines an element $\mathcal A$ of order dividing $8$ of the Brauer group of the curve $f=0$. Its local invariants at an integer solution would have to add up to $0$. We show that they are $\frac12$ at $13$, $17$ and $137$, that they vanish at all other places except $19$, and that $8\inv_{19}\mathcal A$ takes only the values $0,2,3,6,7$ on the $19$-adic integral points; so the sum is never $0$.

Besides the explicit formula for tame Hilbert symbols and the Hilbert reciprocity law, the proof quotes standard facts on Brauer groups of curves and of their regular models over $\Z_p$: residues and their compatibility with corestriction, purity, the reciprocity law for residues on a curve, and the description of the local evaluation maps by the Tate pairing, together with Raynaud's description of the N\'eron model of the Jacobian. Apart from these, it uses polynomial identities modulo the restrictions of $g$ to the lines and finite computations with residues. All their data are listed in Section~\ref{sec:data}. The whole proof is also formalized in Lean~4 in the file \texttt{Solution.lean}; the formal proof does not use the facts on Brauer groups (Section~\ref{sec:lean}).

\section{Hilbert symbols of order 8}\label{sec:symbols}

\paragraph{The field.} Let $\zeta$ be a primitive $8$th root of unity, so that $\zeta^4=-1$, and $K=\Q(\zeta)$. The field $K$ is totally complex of degree $4$, with ring of integers $\Z[\zeta]$; we write its elements as polynomials in $\zeta$ of degree at most $3$, and in the tables of Section~\ref{sec:data} also as vectors $[a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3]=a_0+a_1\zeta+a_2\zeta^2+a_3\zeta^3$. Note that $\sqrt2=\zeta-\zeta^3$. The Galois group of $K/\Q$ is $G=\{\sigma_1,\sigma_3,\sigma_5,\sigma_7\}$, where $\sigma_k(\zeta)=\zeta^k$; we identify $G$ with $(\Z/8\Z)^\times$, and note that $\sigma_k^2=1$ and $k^2\equiv1\pmod 8$ for every $k$.

For a finite place $v$ of $K$ we write $K_v$ for the completion, $v(a)$ for the normalized valuation, and call $a$ a unit at $v$ if $v(a)=0$. An odd prime $p$ is unramified in $K$. If $p\equiv1\pmod8$, there are four places above $p$, with residue field $\F_p$; they correspond to the four roots $r$ of $t^4+1$ modulo $p$, the place $v_r$ being the one at which $\zeta\equiv r$. Otherwise there are two places above $p$, with residue field $\F_{p^2}$; they correspond to the two monic quadratic factors $t^2+at+b$ of $t^4+1$ modulo $p$, $\zeta$ reducing to a root of the factor. The prime $2$ is totally ramified, with uniformizer $\lambda=1-\zeta$.

\paragraph{Hilbert symbols.} For a place $v$ of $K$ and $a,b\in K_v^\times$, the Hilbert symbol $(a,b)_v$ of order $8$ is an $8$th root of unity \cite[Chapter~V, \S3]{N}. We write $(a,b)_v=\zeta^{\beta_v(a,b)}$ with $\beta_v(a,b)\in\Z/8\Z$, and we use the following facts \cite[Chapter~V, \S3 and Chapter~VI, \S8]{N}.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(H1)] $\beta_v(a,bc)=\beta_v(a,b)+\beta_v(a,c)$, $\beta_v(a,b)=-\beta_v(b,a)$, and $\beta_v(a,c^8)=0$.
\item[(H2)] Let $v$ be a finite place not above $2$, let $q$ be the number of elements of its residue field, and let $\varpi$ be a uniformizer at $v$. Write $a=\varpi^eu$ and $b=\varpi^fw$ with units $u$ and $w$, and define $\chi_v(u)\in\Z/8\Z$ by $\bar u^{(q-1)/8}=\bar\zeta^{\,\chi_v(u)}$, where the bar denotes the reduction to the residue field. Then $\beta_v(a,b)=e\,\chi_v(w)-f\,\chi_v(u)+ef\,\chi_v(-1)$. In particular, $\beta_v(a,b)=0$ if $a$ and $b$ are both units.
\item[(H3)] (Hilbert reciprocity.) For $a,b\in K^\times$, $\beta_v(a,b)=0$ for all but finitely many places $v$, and $\sum_v\beta_v(a,b)=0$, where the sum is over all places of $K$. At the complex places, $\beta_v(a,b)=0$.
\end{itemize}
Formula (H2) fixes the normalization of the symbols; with the opposite sign convention all values $\beta_v$ change sign, and the proof below is the same. Applying $\sigma_k$ maps the symbol to its conjugate: $(\sigma_k a,\sigma_k b)_{\sigma_k v}=\sigma_k\bigl((a,b)_v\bigr)$, hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:galois}
\beta_{\sigma_k v}(\sigma_k a,\sigma_k b)=k\,\beta_v(a,b).
\end{equation}

\section{The curve and its Brauer group}\label{sec:curve}

\paragraph{The curve.} Let $U$ be the affine curve $f(x,y)=0$ over $\Q$. In the coordinates $(x,Y)$ it is the curve $g=0$. Its closure $X$ in $\mathbb P^2$, with coordinates $(x:Y:Z)$, is the quartic $Y^3Z+xYZ^2-4x^4+2Z^4=0$. It is smooth: at a singular point of $U$ over $\bar\Q$ we have $g_Y=3Y^2+x=0$ and $g_x=Y-16x^3=0$, which gives $x=-768x^6$; $x=0$ forces $Y=0$ and $g=2$, and otherwise $768x^5=-1$, and $g=0$ becomes $\frac{20}3x^4+2=0$, so that $x=x^5/x^4=5/1152$ and $2\cdot5^5+2^{28}3^9=0$, which is false. The only point of $X$ on the line $Z=0$ is $\infty=(0:1:0)$, at which the derivative with respect to $Z$ is $1$. So $X$ is a smooth plane quartic of genus $3$, and $X\setminus U=\{\infty\}$. The point $Q_0=(x,Y)=(1,1)$, that is $(x,y)=(1,\frac12)$, lies on $U$.

For a prime $p$ we write $U(\Z_p)$ for the set of solutions of $f=0$ with $x,y\in\Z_p$. For odd $p$ these are the solutions of $g=0$ with $x,Y\in\Z_p$; for $p=2$ they are the solutions of $g=0$ with $x\in\Z_2$ and $Y\in2\Z_2$. For an odd prime $p$ let $\mathcal U_p$ be the scheme $g=0$ over $\Z_p$ and $\mathcal X_p$ its closure in $\mathbb P^2_{\Z_p}$, the scheme $Y^3Z+xYZ^2-4x^4+2Z^4=0$; then $U(\Z_p)=\mathcal U_p(\Z_p)$, and $\mathcal X_p(\Z_p)=X(\Q_p)$. For a point $P\in U(\Z_p)$ we call the set of points of $U(\Z_p)$ with the same reduction modulo $p$ the \emph{residue disc} of $P$.

\paragraph{Brauer classes.} For a field $F$ of characteristic $0$ containing $\zeta$ and $a,b\in F^\times$ let $(a,b)\in\Br(F)$ be the class of the cyclic algebra defined by $\zeta$, $a$ and $b$; it is bilinear, $(a,b)=-(b,a)$, and $8(a,b)=0$. For a completion $K_v$, $\inv_v(a,b)=\beta_v(a,b)/8$ with the $\beta_v$ of Section~\ref{sec:symbols}, up to a sign which does not depend on $v$ \cite[Chapter~V, \S3]{N}; we fix the normalization so that the sign is $+$. For a field $F\supseteq K$ let $\kappa\colon F^\times\to H^1(F,\Z/8\Z)$ be the Kummer map with respect to $\zeta$. We use the following standard facts \cite{CTS,P}.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(B1)] Every class $\alpha\in\Br(\Q(X))$ has a residue $\partial_x\alpha\in H^1(\Q(x),\Q/\Z)$ at every closed point $x$ of $X$, and for an open subset $V$ of $X$, $\alpha\in\Br(V)$ if and only if $\partial_x\alpha=0$ for every closed point $x$ of $V$ (purity); a class in $\Br(V)$ can be evaluated at every point of $V$ with values in a field or a completion. More generally, every discrete valuation of a field $F$ whose residue field has characteristic $\neq2$ defines a residue map on $\Br(F)[8]$, and residues commute with corestriction along finite extensions $F'/F$ in which the valuation is unramified: the residue of $\Cor_{F'/F}\beta$ is the sum of the corestrictions of the residues of $\beta$ at the valuations of $F'$ above it; for $F=\Q(X)$, $F'=L(X)$ with $L/\Q$ finite and the valuation of a closed point $x$, this reads $\partial_x\Cor_{L(X)/\Q(X)}\beta=\sum_{y\mapsto x}\Cor_{L(y)/\Q(x)}\partial_y\beta$, the sum over the closed points $y$ of $X_L$ above $x$. At a discrete valuation $w$ of a field containing $\zeta$, with residue characteristic $\neq2$, the residue of $(a,b)$ is the Kummer class of the tame symbol $(-1)^{w(a)w(b)}a^{w(b)}b^{-w(a)}$ reduced modulo $w$, up to a sign which depends only on the normalization \cite[Chapters~6 and~7]{GS}.
\item[(B2)] The corestrictions to $\Q$ of the residues of a class $\alpha\in\Br(\Q(X))$ at all closed points of $X$ add up to $0$.
\item[(B3)] Let $p$ be odd and $\mathcal X$ a regular integral scheme, proper and flat over $\Z_p$, with generic fibre $X\otimes\Q_p$, and let $\alpha\in\Br(X\otimes\Q_p)[8]$. If the residue of $\alpha$ at the generic point of every component of the special fibre of $\mathcal X$ vanishes, then $\alpha$ extends to $\Br(\mathcal X)$ (purity), and then $\inv_p\alpha(P)=0$ for every $P\in X(\Q_p)$, since $P$ extends to a point of $\mathcal X(\Z_p)$ and $\Br(\Z_p)=0$.
\item[(B4)] For $\alpha\in\Br(X)$ and $P\in X(\Q)$, $\alpha(P)\in\Br(\Q)$, so $\sum_v\inv_v\alpha(P)=0$, the sum over all places of $\Q$.
\item[(B5)] Let $V\subseteq X$ be open and $\beta\in\Br(V_K)$. Then $\Cor_{V_K/V}\beta\in\Br(V)$, its image in $\Br(\Q(X))$ is $\Cor_{K(X)/\Q(X)}\beta$, and for every field $F\supseteq\Q$ and $P\in V(F)$, $(\Cor_{V_K/V}\beta)(P)=\Cor_{K\otimes F/F}\beta(P)$, since $V_K\to V$ is finite and \'etale. As $\Br(V)\to\Br(\Q(X))$ is injective, a class of $\Br(X)$ whose image in $\Br(\Q(X))$ is $\Cor_{K(X)/\Q(X)}\beta$ restricts to $\Cor_{V_K/V}\beta$ on $V$. For a completion $\Q_p$, $\inv_p\Cor_{K\otimes\Q_p/\Q_p}\gamma=\sum_{w\mid p}\inv_w\gamma_w$.
\end{itemize}

\section{The certificate}\label{sec:cert}

\paragraph{The set $S$ and the generators.} Let $S$ consist of the $28$ primes
\begin{gather*}
2,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 11,\ 13,\ 17,\ 19,\ 23,\ 41,\ 73,\ 89,\ 97,\ 113,\\
137,\ 193,\ 233,\ 241,\ 257,\ 281,\ 313,\ 337,\ 353,\ 401,\ 409,\ 433,\ 449,\ 457.
\end{gather*}
These are the primes up to $23$ and the twenty primes $p\equiv1\pmod8$ up to $457$. There are $95$ places of $K$ above $S$. Table~\ref{tab:gens} lists $97$ elements $g_1,\dots,g_{97}$ of $\Z[\zeta]$: the root of unity $g_1=\zeta$, the unit $g_2=1+\sqrt2=1+\zeta-\zeta^3$, the element $g_3=-\zeta+\zeta^2=-\zeta\lambda$ of valuation $1$ at the place above $2$, and for each of the other $94$ places $w$ a generator $g_i$ of its prime ideal, so that $w(g_i)=1$ and $w'(g_i)=0$ at all other places $w'$. We call this place the place of $g_i$. The $g_i$ generate the $S$-units of $K$; the constants below are products of them.

\paragraph{Lines.} The certificate consists of 824 \emph{representative lines} $l=0,\dots,823$, given by linear forms
\[
H_l=A_lx+B_lY+C_l,\qquad A_l,B_l,C_l\in\Z[\zeta],
\]
with either $B_l=1$ (791 lines) or $A_l=1$, $B_l=0$ (33 \emph{vertical} lines), and of constants $b_l=\prod_ig_i^{e_{l,i}}$ with $0\leq e_{l,i}\leq7$ (Table~\ref{tab:lines}). The conjugate lines $\sigma_k(l)$, $k\in G$, are the lines with the forms $\sigma_k(H_l)$, where $\sigma_k$ acts on the coefficients. We check that these $3296$ lines are pairwise distinct. On a line $j$ we use the parameter $t=x$ if $B_j=1$, and $t=Y$ if $j$ is vertical; we write $f_j(t)$ for the restriction of $g$ to $j$, of degree $4$, respectively $3$ (the fourth point of a vertical line on $X$ is $\infty$).

\paragraph{Anchors and stars.} The certificate also contains 26615 \emph{anchors}: points $P\in K^2$ with $g(P)\neq0$. No two of them are conjugate, and none is fixed by a $\sigma_k\neq\sigma_1$. Each anchor has a \emph{star}: distinct lines $j_0,j_1,\dots,j_m$ through $P$, $m\geq1$, each of them a conjugate $j_e=\sigma_{k_e}(l_e)$ of a representative line, with weights $w_0,\dots,w_m\in\Z/8\Z$ such that $\sum_ew_e=0$. Table~\ref{tab:anchors} lists the stars; the anchor is the common point of the lines of its star. The line $j_0$ is the \emph{centre} of the star, and the pairs $\{j_e,j_0\}$, $e\geq1$, are its \emph{edges}; there are 42512 edges in all, and 69127 entries $(l_e,k_e,w_e)$.

For lines $j\neq j'$ through $P$, the restriction of $H_{j'}$ to $j$ is $\lambda(j,j')(t-t_P)$, where $t_P$ is the parameter of $P$ on $j$ and
\[
\lambda(j,j')=\begin{cases}A_{j'}-B_{j'}A_j&\text{if }B_j=1,\\ B_{j'}&\text{if $j$ is vertical,}\end{cases}
\]
with $A_j,B_j$ the coefficients of the form of $j$; $\lambda(j,j')\neq0$, since $j$ and $j'$ are distinct lines through $P$.

\paragraph{The class.} Write $(a,b)$ for the symbol of Section~\ref{sec:curve} over the function field $K(X)$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta}
\beta_0=\sum_P\sum_{e\geq1}w_e\,(H_{j_e},H_{j_0})+\sum_l(H_l,c_l)\in\Br(K(X)),\qquad \mathcal A=\Cor_{K(X)/\Q(X)}\beta_0\in\Br(\Q(X)),
\end{equation}
the first sum over the anchors and the edges of their stars, the second over the representative lines, where
\[
c_l=b_l\prod\sigma_{k_e}\bigl(\lambda(j_e,j_0)\bigr)^{-k_ew_e}\prod\sigma_{k_0}\bigl(\lambda(j_0,j_e)\bigr)^{k_0w_e};
\]
the first product runs over the edges $\{j_e,j_0\}$ (at all anchors) with $l_e=l$, and the second over the edges whose centre $j_0$ is a conjugate of $l$, $j_0=\sigma_{k_0}(l)$.

\paragraph{The vertex identities.} For a representative line $l$ and a point $P$ on $l$ put
\[
D_l(P)=\sum k_ew_e\in\Z/8\Z,
\]
the sum over the entries $e$ of the stars (centres included) at the anchors $P'$ with $j_e=\sigma_{k_e}(l)$ and $\sigma_{k_e}(P')=P$; since $\sigma_{k_e}$ is an involution, $j_e$ passes through $P'$ if and only if $l$ passes through $\sigma_{k_e}(P')$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:El}
E_l=b_l\prod_P(t-t_P)^{D_l(P)}\in K[t]/(f_l),
\end{equation}
the product over the points $P$ on $l$ with $D_l(P)\neq0$, each exponent taken in $\{-3,\dots,4\}$.

\section{The class is unramified}\label{sec:unram}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:orbit}
Suppose that every $f_l$ is squarefree and that $E_l$ is an $8$th power in $K[t]/(f_l)$ for every representative line $l$. Then $\mathcal A\in\Br(U)[8]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $a,b\in K(X)^\times$ we have $\Cor_{K/\Q}(\sigma_ka,\sigma_kb)=k\Cor_{K/\Q}(a,b)$: applying $\sigma_k$ to the coefficients of the cyclic algebra $(a,b)$ gives the cyclic algebra of $\sigma_ka$ and $\sigma_kb$ with respect to $\zeta^k$, which is $k^{-1}(\sigma_ka,\sigma_kb)$, and corestriction is invariant under the automorphism $\sigma_k$ of $K(X)$ over $\Q(X)$; here $k^{-1}\equiv k\pmod8$. As $\sigma_k^{-1}=\sigma_k$, $\mathcal A$ does not change if the constant symbols in $c_l$ are moved back to the lines on which they arise, that is, if $\beta_0$ is replaced by
\[
\beta_0'=\sum_P\sum_{e\geq1}w_e\bigl[(H_{j_e},H_{j_0})-(H_{j_e},\lambda(j_e,j_0))+(H_{j_0},\lambda(j_0,j_e))\bigr]+\sum_l(H_l,b_l).
\]
Two lines of a star meet only at its anchor, which is not on $X$, and a line $j$ vanishes to order $1$ at its points on $U_K$, since $f_j$ is squarefree. So, by the tame symbol (B1), the bracket for the edge $e$ has residue $w_e\,\kappa(t-t_P)$ at the points of $U_K$ on $j_e$, residue $-w_e\,\kappa(t-t_P)$ at the points on $j_0$, and no other residues on $U_K$; here the residue at a point $y$ on a line $j$ is written as the Kummer class of a function on $j$ evaluated at $y$, up to a sign fixed by the normalization. Since the weights of a star add up to $0$, the centre receives $w_0\,\kappa(t-t_P)$. Hence $\partial_y\beta_0'=\sum_{j\ni y}\kappa(\varepsilon_j(y))$ for every closed point $y$ of $U_K$, where $j$ runs over the lines through $y$ and $\varepsilon_j$ is the product of the $(t-t_P)^{w_e}$ over the entries $e$ with $j_e=j$, times $b_l$ if $j=l$ is a representative line.

Let $x$ be a closed point of $U$. By (B1), $\partial_x\mathcal A=\sum_{y\mid x}\Cor_{K(y)/\Q(x)}\partial_y\beta_0'$, the sum over the closed points of $U_K$ above $x$. The automorphism $\tilde\sigma_k$ of $X_K$ over $X$ induced by $\sigma_k$ maps the points above $x$ on $l$ bijectively to those on $\sigma_k(l)$, and for $a\in K(\tilde\sigma_ky)^\times$ we have $\Cor_{K(\tilde\sigma_ky)/\Q(x)}\kappa(a)=k\Cor_{K(y)/\Q(x)}\kappa(\tilde\sigma_k^{-1}a)$, for the same reason as above. Applied to $a=\varepsilon_{\sigma_k(l)}(\tilde\sigma_ky)$, with $\tilde\sigma_k^{-1}a=(\sigma_k\varepsilon_{\sigma_k(l)})(y)$ and $\sigma_k(t-t_{P'})=t-t_{\sigma_kP'}$ on $l$, this gives
\[
\partial_x\mathcal A=\sum_l\ \sum_{y\mid x,\ y\in l}\Cor_{K(y)/\Q(x)}\kappa\Bigl(\prod_k\bigl(\sigma_k\varepsilon_{\sigma_k(l)}\bigr)^k(y)\Bigr)=\sum_l\ \sum_{y\mid x,\ y\in l}\Cor_{K(y)/\Q(x)}\kappa\bigl(E_l(y)\bigr),
\]
the outer sum over the representative lines; here we use that the conjugate lines are pairwise distinct, so that every line through $y$ is $\sigma_k(l)$ for exactly one pair $(l,k)$. Since $f_l$ is squarefree, $K[t]/(f_l)=\prod_yK(y)$ over the points $y$ of $U_K$ on $l$, so $E_l(y)\in K(y)^{\times8}$ and $\partial_x\mathcal A=0$. By (B1), $\mathcal A\in\Br(U)$, and $8\mathcal A=0$ because $8\beta_0=0$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{The witnesses.} For a representative line $l$ write $t_P=n_P/d_P$ with $n_P\in\Z[\zeta]$ and an integer $d_P\geq1$ whose gcd with the coefficients of $n_P$ is $1$, and put
\[
N_l=\prod_{D_l(P)>0}(d_Pt-n_P)^{D_l(P)},\qquad M_l=\prod_{D_l(P)<0}(d_Pt-n_P)^{-D_l(P)},\qquad q_l=\prod_pp^{\langle e_p\rangle},
\]
with $e_p=-\sum_PD_l(P)v_p(d_P)$ and $\langle e_p\rangle\in\{0,\dots,7\}$, $\langle e_p\rangle\equiv e_p\pmod8$. Then $q_lb_lN_l/M_l$ is $E_l$ times the $8$th power of a non-zero rational number. Table~\ref{tab:roots} lists, for every representative line, an element $r_l=R_l(t)/\delta_l$ with $R_l\in\Z[\zeta][t]$ of degree less than $\deg f_l$ and an integer $\delta_l\geq1$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:witness}
M_l\,r_l^8\equiv q_lb_l\,N_l\pmod{f_l}\quad\text{in }K[t].
\end{equation}
Since no $t_P$ with $D_l(P)\neq0$ is a root of $f_l$ (the anchors are not on $X$), $M_l$ is invertible modulo $f_l$, and \eqref{eq:witness} shows that $E_l$ is an $8$th power in $K[t]/(f_l)$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:unram}
The class $\mathcal A$ lies in $\Br(X)[8]$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The following finite computations with exact arithmetic verify the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:orbit}, and the facts used in Section~\ref{sec:cert}.
\begin{itemize}
\item The $3296$ conjugate lines are pairwise distinct. Every line $j_e$ of a star passes through its anchor, the lines of a star are distinct, the weights of every star add up to $0$ in $\Z/8\Z$, and $g(P)\neq0$ at every anchor. No two anchors are conjugate, and no anchor is fixed by a $\sigma_k\neq\sigma_1$.
\item Every $f_l$ is squarefree. Over $K$, $f_l$ is irreducible of degree $4$ for $783$ lines and irreducible of degree $3$ for the $33$ vertical lines; for the $8$ lines $l=10,\,68,\,229,\,349,\,505,\,536,\,567,\,746$, which pass through $Q_0$, it is $t-1$ times an irreducible cubic.
\item The identity \eqref{eq:witness} holds for every representative line, with the data of Tables~\ref{tab:lines}, \ref{tab:anchors} and~\ref{tab:roots}.
\item The $97$ generators are $S$-units, and so are the leading coefficients $\lambda(j,j')$ for all $89161$ pairs of lines through a common anchor: their norms are $S$-units, the largest being $625$. Hence the constants $c_l$ are $S$-units.
\end{itemize}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:orbit}, $\mathcal A\in\Br(U)[8]$, so the residues of $\mathcal A$ at all closed points of $U$ vanish. The only other closed point of $X$ is the rational point $\infty$, so by (B2) the residue of $\mathcal A$ at $\infty$ vanishes as well, and $\mathcal A\in\Br(X)$ by (B1).
\end{proof}

\section{Reduction modulo primes}\label{sec:reduction}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:bad}
Let $p$ be an odd prime. If $p\notin\{13,50021,4062613\}$, then $\mathcal X_p$ is smooth over $\Z_p$. If $p\in\{13,50021,4062613\}$, then the special fibre of $\mathcal X_p$ has exactly one singular point, a node, which lies on $\mathcal U_p$ and at which $\mathcal X_p$ is regular, and no point of $U(\Z_p)$ reduces to it. For every odd $p$ the special fibre of $\mathcal X_p$ is geometrically integral. So $\mathcal X_p$ is regular, integral, proper and flat over $\Z_p$, with generic fibre $X\otimes\Q_p$ and geometrically integral special fibre, and every point of $U(\Z_p)$ reduces to a smooth point of the special fibre.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A singular point of the special fibre over $\bar\F_p$ satisfies $Y=16x^3$ and $x=-3Y^2$, hence $x=-768x^6$. If $x=0$ then $Y=0$ and $g=2\neq0$. If $p=3$ this is the only possibility. If $p=5$, then $x^5=-1/768=3$, so $x=3$, $Y=16\cdot27\equiv2$, and $g(3,2)\equiv2\pmod5$. For $p\geq7$, as in Section~\ref{sec:curve}, $x=5/1152$, $Y=16x^3$, and $p$ divides $5^5+2^{27}3^9=13\cdot50021\cdot4062613$. Conversely, for these three primes the point $c=(5/1152,16(5/1152)^3)\in\Q^2$ satisfies $g_x(c)=0$ and $p\mid g_Y(c)$, and $g(c)$ has $p$-adic valuation exactly $1$; the reduction of $c$ is a node, since the Hessian determinant $g_{xx}g_{YY}-g_{xY}^2=-288x^2Y-1$ is $-4608x_c^5-1\equiv5\not\equiv0\pmod p$ at $c$, by $768x_c^5\equiv-1$. Let $\mathfrak m=(p,x-x_c,Y-Y_c)$ be the maximal ideal of the local ring of the affine plane over $\Z_p$ at the reduction of $c=(x_c,Y_c)$. Since $g_x(c)=0$ and $p\mid g_Y(c)$, the Taylor expansion of $g$ at $c$ gives $g\equiv g(c)\pmod{\mathfrak m^2}$, and $g(c)\notin\mathfrak m^2$ because $v_p(g(c))=1$; so $\mathcal U_p$ is regular there. Every lift $c'$ of the node satisfies $g(c')\equiv g(c)\not\equiv0\pmod{p^2}$ for the same reason, so no point of $U(\Z_p)$ reduces to it; for $p=13$ the node is $(x,Y)\equiv(12,10)$. Finally, for odd $p$ the line $Z=0$ meets the special fibre of $\mathcal X_p$ only at $\infty$, where the derivative of $Y^3Z+xYZ^2-4x^4+2Z^4$ with respect to $Z$ is $1$, so that $\mathcal X_p$ is smooth over $\Z_p$ there. Every component of a plane curve meets this line, and only one component passes through a smooth point, with multiplicity $1$; so the special fibre of $\mathcal X_p$ is geometrically integral. As a hypersurface in $\mathbb P^2_{\Z_p}$ defined by a polynomial whose reduction modulo $p$ is non-zero, $\mathcal X_p$ is flat over $\Z_p$; it is proper, regular by the above, and integral, since it is flat with integral generic fibre $X\otimes\Q_p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:outside}
Let $p$ be an odd prime such that $w(c_l)\equiv0\pmod8$ for every representative line $l$ and every place $w$ of $K$ above $p$. Then $\inv_p\mathcal A(P)=0$ for every $P\in X(\Q_p)$, in particular for every $P\in U(\Z_p)$. This holds for every odd prime $p\notin S$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:bad}, $\mathcal X_p$ is regular, proper and flat over $\Z_p$, with geometrically integral special fibre $\mathcal X_0$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:unram}, $\mathcal A\in\Br(X)[8]$. By (B3) it suffices to show that the residue of $\mathcal A$ at the generic point $\eta$ of $\mathcal X_0$ vanishes. By (B1) for the extension $K\otimes\Q_p=\prod_{w\mid p}K_w$, this residue is $\sum_{w\mid p}\Cor\partial_{\eta_w}\beta_0$, where $\eta_w$ is the generic point of the special fibre over the ring of integers of $K_w$; since $K_w/\Q_p$ is unramified, $p$ is a uniformizer at $\eta_w$, and the valuation at $\eta_w$ extends $w$. The forms $H_j$ have coefficients in $\Z[\zeta]$ and $B_j=1$ or $A_j=1$, so they are non-zero modulo $w$, and as linear forms they do not vanish on the integral quartic $\mathcal X_0$; so they are units at $\eta_w$. Write $c_l=p^{8m_{l,w}}u_{l,w}$ with $m_{l,w}\in\Z$ and $u_{l,w}$ a unit at $w$; then $(H_l,c_l)=(H_l,u_{l,w})+8m_{l,w}(H_l,p)=(H_l,u_{l,w})$ in $\Br(K_w(X))$. So all entries of the symbols in \eqref{eq:beta}, after this replacement, are units at $\eta_w$, their tame symbols are trivial ($p$ is odd), and $\partial_{\eta_w}\beta_0=0$. For $p\notin S$ the hypothesis holds with $w(c_l)=0$, because the $g_i$ and the $\lambda(j,j')$ are $S$-units (Proposition~\ref{prop:unram}), so the constants $c_l$ are $S$-units.
\end{proof}

\section{Local values at the primes of \texorpdfstring{$S$}{S}}\label{sec:local}

\paragraph{The Tate pairing.} Let $J$ be the Jacobian of $X$ and $\iota\colon X\to J$, $P\mapsto[P-\infty]$. Since $\mathcal A\in\Br(X)$ and $8\mathcal A=0$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:unram}), there are $\xi\in H^1(\Q,J)[8]$ and constants $\gamma_v\in\Q/\Z$ such that
\[
\inv_v\mathcal A(P)=\langle\iota(P),\xi_v\rangle_v+\gamma_v\qquad\text{for every place $v$ and every $P\in X(\Q_v)$,}
\]
where $\xi_v$ is the restriction of $\xi$ to $\Q_v$ and $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_v\colon J(\Q_v)\times H^1(\Q_v,J)\to\Q/\Z$ is the local Tate pairing \cite{Sk,St}; a sign in this compatibility can be absorbed into $\xi$. (Since $X(\Q)\neq\emptyset$, $\Br(X)/\Br(\Q)\cong H^1(\Q,\operatorname{Pic}X_{\bar\Q})\cong H^1(\Q,J)$.)

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:disc}
Let $p$ be an odd prime. Then $\inv_p\mathcal A$ is constant on every residue disc of $U(\Z_p)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $P,P'\in U(\Z_p)$ have the same reduction $\bar P$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:bad}, $\mathcal X_p$ is regular, proper and flat over $\Z_p$ with geometrically integral special fibre, and $\bar P$ is a smooth point of the special fibre. The closures $\mathcal P,\mathcal P'$ of $P,P'$ in $\mathcal X_p$ are sections through the smooth locus; as $\mathcal X_p$ is regular, $\mathcal P-\mathcal P'$ is a Cartier divisor, and $\mathcal O(\mathcal P-\mathcal P')$ defines a point of $\operatorname{Pic}^0_{\mathcal X_p/\Z_p}(\Z_p)$ with generic fibre $\iota(P)-\iota(P')$ and trivial special fibre, since $\bar P=\bar P'$. By Raynaud's theorem \cite[Section~9.5, Theorem~4]{BLR}, whose hypotheses hold here ($\mathcal X_p$ is regular, proper and flat over $\Z_p$, its generic fibre $X\otimes\Q_p$ is smooth and geometrically connected, its special fibre is geometrically integral, so the gcd of the multiplicities of its components is $1$, and $\F_p$ is perfect), $\operatorname{Pic}^0_{\mathcal X_p/\Z_p}$ is the identity component $\mathcal N^0$ of the N\'eron model of $J$ over $\Z_p$. So $\iota(P)-\iota(P')$ lies in the kernel of the reduction map $\mathcal N^0(\Z_p)\to\mathcal N^0(\F_p)$, which is a pro-$p$ group; as $p$ is odd, $\iota(P)-\iota(P')=8R$ with $R\in J(\Q_p)$. Hence $\inv_p\mathcal A(P)-\inv_p\mathcal A(P')=\langle8R,\xi_p\rangle_p=\langle R,8\xi_p\rangle_p=0$.
\end{proof}

Let $\mathcal O=\Z_2[\zeta]$ and $U^{(n)}=1+\lambda^n\mathcal O$, and let $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_6$ be the elements $\lambda,\ \zeta,\ 1+\lambda,\ 1+\lambda^2,\ 1+\lambda^3,\ 1+\lambda^4$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:two}
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $U^{(17)}\subseteq K_\lambda^{\times8}$, the classes of $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_6$ form a basis of $K_\lambda^\times/K_\lambda^{\times8}\cong(\Z/8\Z)^6$, and $\beta_\lambda(a,b)=L(a)^{\mathsf T}M\,L(b)$, where $L(a)\in(\Z/8\Z)^6$ is the coordinate vector of $a$ in this basis and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:M}
M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 & 5\\0 & 0 & 2 & 1 & 2 & 3\\0 & 6 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 7\\6 & 7 & 7 & 4 & 1 & 2\\0 & 6 & 7 & 7 & 0 & 0\\3 & 5 & 1 & 6 & 0 & 4\end{pmatrix}\pmod8
\end{equation}
is the matrix of the symbols $\beta_\lambda(\theta_i,\theta_j)$.
\item[(ii)] For every $P\in U(\Z_2)$, $x(P)$ is odd, and for every odd $a\in\Z_2$ there is exactly one $P_a\in U(\Z_2)$ with $x(P_a)=a$. If $4k\geq\max_jv_\lambda(H_j(P_a))+17$, the maximum over all conjugate lines $j$, then $\inv_2\mathcal A$ is constant on the points $P\in U(\Z_2)$ with $x(P)\equiv a\pmod{2^k}$.
\end{itemize}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) For $n\geq5$ the logarithm identifies $U^{(n)}$ with $\lambda^n\mathcal O$, and $8\mathcal O=\lambda^{12}\mathcal O$; so $U^{(17)}=(U^{(5)})^8$. The units of $\mathcal O$ form $\mu_8\times\Z_2^4$, so $\mathcal O^\times/\mathcal O^{\times8}$ has $8^5$ elements. The image of $\mathcal O^{\times8}$ in $\mathcal O^\times/U^{(17)}$ is generated by the $8$th powers of the generators $1+\lambda^i$, $1\leq i\leq16$, of $\mathcal O^\times/U^{(17)}$ (and $\zeta^8=1$), and it has order $2$, since $[\mathcal O^\times:U^{(17)}]=2^{16}$ and $[\mathcal O^\times:\mathcal O^{\times8}]=2^{15}$. A direct enumeration shows that the $8^5$ products of $\theta_2,\dots,\theta_6$, together with their products with the non-trivial element of this image, are the $2^{16}$ elements of $\mathcal O^\times/U^{(17)}$. This proves the basis property, and the formula for $\beta_\lambda$ follows by (H1). The entries of $M$ follow from (H3): for each pair $(\theta_i,\theta_j)$ of elements of $K$, $\beta_\lambda(\theta_i,\theta_j)$ is minus the sum of the $\beta_v(\theta_i,\theta_j)$ over the finite places $v\nmid2$, which are given by (H2). The norms of $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_6$ are $2,1,17,9,17,153$, so only the places above $3$ and $17$ contribute.

(ii) If $x$ is even and $Y\in2\Z_2$, then $g(x,Y)\equiv2\pmod4$; so $x$ is odd. For odd $a$, $f(a,y)\equiv ay+1\pmod 2$ forces $y$ to be odd, and $f_y=12y^2+a$ is odd, so by Hensel's lemma there is exactly one $y\in\Z_2$ with $f(a,y)=0$. If $x(P)\equiv a\pmod{2^k}$, then $y(P)\equiv y(P_a)\pmod{2^k}$, so $H_j(P)-H_j(P_a)\in2^k\mathcal O=\lambda^{4k}\mathcal O$ and $H_j(P)/H_j(P_a)\in U^{(17)}$ for every line; in particular $H_j(P)$ has the same valuation as $H_j(P_a)$ and is non-zero. So every entry of every symbol in \eqref{eq:beta} changes by an $8$th power, and $8\inv_2\mathcal A(P)=b_2(P)$ (see \eqref{eq:bp} below) does not change.
\end{proof}

For $P\in U(\Q_p)$ at which no $H_j$ vanishes put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bp}
b_p(P)=\sum_{w\mid p}\Bigl(\sum_P\sum_{e\geq1}w_e\,\beta_w\bigl(H_{j_e}(P),H_{j_0}(P)\bigr)+\sum_l\beta_w\bigl(H_l(P),c_l\bigr)\Bigr)\in\Z/8\Z,
\end{equation}
the sum over the places $w$ of $K$ above $p$ (the inner sums as in \eqref{eq:beta}). Let $V\subseteq U$ be the complement of the zeros of all the conjugate lines; it is defined over $\Q$, the set of lines being stable under $G$, and $\beta_0\in\Br(V_K)$ by (B1) for the curve $X_K$, since all entries of its symbols are units at the closed points of $V_K$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:unram} and (B5), $\mathcal A$ restricts to $\Cor_{V_K/V}\beta_0$ on $V$, so $8\inv_p\mathcal A(P)=b_p(P)$ for every $P\in U(\Q_p)$ at which no $H_j$ vanishes.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:local}
For every $P\in U(\Z_p)$, $8\inv_p\mathcal A(P)$ is $4$ for $p=13,17,137$, and $0$ for every other prime $p\neq19$. On $U(\Z_{19})$, $8\inv_{19}\mathcal A$ takes the values $0,2,3,6,7$, according to the reduction of the point modulo $19$ (Table~\ref{tab:nineteen}). At the real place $\inv_\infty\mathcal A=0$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For odd $p\notin S$ this is Proposition~\ref{prop:outside}. At the real place, $\Br(\mathbb C(X))=0$ by Tsen's theorem, so the image of $\mathcal A$ in $\Br(\mathbb R(X))$, which by (B5) is a corestriction from $\mathbb R(X)\otimes_\Q K\cong\mathbb C(X)^2$, vanishes; as $\Br(X_{\mathbb R})\to\Br(\mathbb R(X))$ is injective, $\mathcal A=0$ in $\Br(X_{\mathbb R})$ and $\inv_\infty\mathcal A=0$. For the primes of $S$ we use the following computations.
\begin{itemize}
\item For the $10$ primes $p=23,\,281,\,313,\,337,\,353,\,401,\,409,\,433,\,449,\,457$, $w(c_l)\equiv0\pmod8$ for every representative line $l$ and every place $w$ above $p$; this is a finite computation with the data of Tables~\ref{tab:gens}, \ref{tab:lines} and~\ref{tab:anchors}. So $\inv_p\mathcal A=0$ on $U(\Z_p)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:outside}.
\item Let $p$ be one of the other $17$ odd primes of $S$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:bad}, every point of $U(\Z_p)$ reduces to a smooth point of the special fibre of $\mathcal X_p$, and by Hensel's lemma every smooth point $\bar P$ of the special fibre in $\mathcal U_p(\F_p)$ is the reduction of a point of $U(\Z_p)$: if $g_Y(\bar P)\neq0$, fix $x$ to be an integer lifting $\bar x$ and solve $g=0$ for $Y$, and otherwise fix $Y$ and solve for $x$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:disc}, $8\inv_p\mathcal A$ is constant on the residue disc of $\bar P$, so it suffices to compute $b_p$ at one such lift $\tilde P$. We computed $\tilde P$ modulo $p^N$ with $p^N>10^{130}$, and $b_p(\tilde P)$ by \eqref{eq:bp} and (H2), for all $1585$ smooth points (Table~\ref{tab:oddvalues}). At every lift the valuations $w(H_j(\tilde P))$ of all conjugate lines are smaller than $N$, so no $H_j$ vanishes at $\tilde P$ and (H2) determines $b_p(\tilde P)$ exactly. (Two further lifts of every residue disc gave the same values.) The result is that $8\inv_p\mathcal A$ is $4$ on all of $U(\Z_p)$ for $p=13,17,137$, $0$ for the other primes $p\neq19$, and Table~\ref{tab:nineteen} gives the values at $19$.
\item At $2$, the $80$ classes $a\bmod2^k$ of Table~\ref{tab:two}, with $k=7$ or $8$, cover all odd $a$, and at each of them the condition of Lemma~\ref{lem:two}(ii) holds (with $\max_jv_\lambda(H_j(P_a))\leq12$). The value $b_2(P_a)$, computed with Lemma~\ref{lem:two}(i), is $0$ at all of them.
\end{itemize}
This proves the proposition.
\end{proof}

\section{Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}}\label{sec:proof}

Suppose that $(x,y)\in\Z^2$ satisfies $f(x,y)=0$, and let $P=(x,y)\in U(\Q)$. Then $P\in U(\Z_p)$ for every prime $p$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:unram}, $\mathcal A(P)\in\Br(\Q)$ is defined, and by (B4), $\sum_v8\inv_v\mathcal A(P)=0$ in $\Z/8\Z$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:local},
\[
\sum_v8\inv_v\mathcal A(P)=4+4+4+s=4+s,\qquad s=8\inv_{19}\mathcal A(P)\in\{0,2,3,6,7\},
\]
so the sum takes one of the values $4,6,7,2,3$, never $0$. This contradiction proves Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. \qed

\section{Verification and formalization}\label{sec:lean}

\paragraph{Computations.} All identities and local values above were computed with exact arithmetic, by two programs: our own, and a program written independently from a description of the certificate. The latter checked the identities by computing all $8$th roots of $E_l$ in the fields defined by the irreducible factors of $f_l$, and the local values by evaluating \eqref{eq:bp} with (H2) at one lift of every smooth point modulo $p$, for all $27$ odd primes of $S$ (it finds the value $0$ at the ten primes of Proposition~\ref{prop:local} as well), and at $2$ by Hilbert reciprocity (H3) at integral approximations of the points $P_a$. As a cross-check, which is not used in the proof, our own program computed the values at the odd primes of $S$ in a different way, from the reductions of the lines and the valuations $w(c_l)$, by the residue of $\mathcal A$ along the special fibre (the method of Bright~\cite{Br} for regular models). The two programs agree at every point and every class. The witnesses of Table~\ref{tab:roots} were also checked as chains of multiplications in $\Z[\zeta][T]/(F)$ with a monic polynomial $F$ ($T=4t$, $F(T)=-64f_l(T/4)$ if $B_l=1$, and $F=f_l$ for a vertical line), which needs no division. The data of Section~\ref{sec:data} were finally read back from the source of this file and compared with the data of the computations.

\paragraph{Lean.} The file \texttt{Solution.lean} proves Theorem~\ref{thm:main} in Lean~4 with Mathlib, for the same certificate; its proof uses only the axioms \texttt{propext}, \texttt{Quot.sound} and \texttt{Classical.choice}, and \texttt{comparator} checks that it proves exactly the statement of \texttt{Challenge.lean}. The formal proof does not use the facts on Brauer groups of Section~\ref{sec:curve} or the Tate pairing. It proves the product formula (H3) for Hilbert symbols of order $8$ within a development of local and global class field theory contained in the file, and it evaluates the symbols of \eqref{eq:bp} at an integer solution directly: at the primes outside $S$ it shows that the sum vanishes, using the identities \eqref{eq:witness} and the data of the anchors, and at the primes of $S$ it computes the values on explicit finite covers of the integral points by residue classes, at all $27$ odd primes of $S$ and at $2$. The file is large (about $95$ MB).

\clearpage
